area: Area VII. Slow Flight and Stalls
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why a wing stalls above its 1 G stall speed in a turn or pull-up, and fly an accelerated stall the way the commercial ACS asks: a coordinated 45° bank, entered at or below VA, back pressure increased smoothly to an impending stall, then a prompt recovery, climb at VX or VY, and return to the assigned altitude, heading and airspeed, all finished no lower than 3,000 feet AGL.
why: Accelerated stalls happen at higher airspeeds and often at lower pitch attitudes than pilots expect, so they surprise people, and they tend to be more aggressive than 1 G stalls [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Most happen by accident in botched turns, stall recoveries, dive pullouts and base-to-final overshoots [[24:124|AFH 5-19]], which is why the commercial applicant is asked to show one.

prereading.what: Accelerated stalls: what they are, where they happen, VA and VO, the two entry methods, how the stall behaves and the recovery. Read this twice.
prereading.label: AFH 5-19 to 5-20

prereading.what: Impending and full stalls, the four limits on a published stall speed, stall characteristics and the stall recovery template.
prereading.label: AFH 5-12 to 5-16

prereading.what: Secondary stalls, the common stall errors list, and how a stall plus yaw becomes a spin.
prereading.label: AFH 5-18 to 5-22

prereading.what: Stalls at any speed: the high-speed pull-up and the level turn, and how the airplane pitches down at the stall.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-25 to 5-26

prereading.what: Load factor and stall speed, design maneuvering speed, high-speed stalls, stall and spin recovery loads, and the Vg diagram.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-34 to 5-38

prereading.what: Stall and spin awareness: load factor, CG, weight, turbulence, distractions, recognition, recovery, secondary stalls and the primary cause of spins.
prereading.label: AC 61-67C 100 to 109

prereading.what: Three real-world traps: slip versus skid stalls, the accelerated stall in a hurried round out, and the turnback after an engine failure.
prereading.label: AFH 9-13, 9-31, 18-7

warmup: Think first: your airplane's book stall speed is 48 knots. You are doing 75 knots, the nose is above the horizon, and a moment later the wing buffets and the nose drops. Nothing broke, and you were far above 48 knots. What did you change to make the wing stall, and why did the book number not protect you?

key_terms.def: Any stall that happens while the G-load is above +1 G, as in a turn, pull-up or other abrupt change in flightpath. It comes at a higher indicated airspeed than the 1 G stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
The angle of attack where the airflow separates and the wing stalls. A given wing always stalls at this same angle, whatever the airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
The lift the wings make divided by the airplane's actual weight, given in Gs. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].
The angle of attack has set off a stall warning but has not yet reached the critical angle. Cues include buffet, a stick shaker or an aural warning [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
The critical angle of attack is exceeded. Typically the nose drops on its own and cannot be readily stopped, sometimes with an uncommanded roll [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

The highest speed at which the positive design limit load can be reached by gusts or by full deflection of one control surface without structural damage. It goes down as weight goes down [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].
A chart of load factor against airspeed for one airplane at one weight and altitude. Its curved line of maximum lift is labeled accelerated stall [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]] [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]].
A stall that happens after recovery from an earlier stall, usually because the pilot pulls the nose up too soon or tries to break the stall with power only [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
A stall with aileron pressure one way and rudder pressure the other. It can come with very little warning and roll toward inverted, the start of a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
An aggravated stall with autorotation: the airplane follows a downward corkscrew path with at least one wing stalled. It needs both a stall and yaw [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].
A twist built into the wing so the tips fly at a slightly lower angle of attack than the roots. The roots stall first and the ailerons keep some effect [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].
A nose-low, descending turn in which the airplane is not stalled, so airspeed and G-load can build fast, often after a botched turn [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

chunks.title: The accelerated stall at commercial standards

body.p: An accelerated stall is any stall that happens when the airplane is loaded above +1 G, such as in a turn or a pull-up. The aim of practicing one is to learn how your airplane stalls at speeds above the 1 G stall speed, and to recover by instinct the moment it starts. Only commercial and flight instructor applicants may be asked to fly it on a practical test, but every pilot should know how it happens [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

The commercial ACS makes it a full Task (power-on or power-off). The private ACS does not; it lists accelerated stalls only as risk items under the power-off and power-on stall Tasks (ACS PA.VII.B.R5, PA.VII.C.R5) and as knowledge under steep turns (ACS PA.V.A.K2d).

head: What the examiner asks
Where it comes from
rows: Pick an entry altitude so the Task is finished no lower than 3,000 ft AGL
ACS CA.VII.D.S2
Set the configuration the examiner asks for
ACS CA.VII.D.S3
Set power so airspeed does not exceed VA or any other POH/AFM limit
ACS CA.VII.D.S4
Hold a coordinated 45° bank and add back pressure smoothly and firmly until an impending stall
ACS CA.VII.D.S5
Acknowledge the first stall cue, recover per the POH, accelerate to VX or VY, return to the assigned altitude, heading and airspeed
ACS CA.VII.D.S6 to S9

callout.text: Never practice accelerated stalls with the flaps extended, because the design G-load limits are lower in that configuration. Use about 45° of bank and never more than the manufacturer's recommended speed, VA or VO [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

body.p: Notice two things the ACS does not give: a plus or minus tolerance on the 45° bank, and an altitude loss limit for the recovery. The examiner judges these. The ACS also asks only for an impending stall in this Task, not a full stall (ACS CA.VII.D.S5).

check.q: On the commercial checkride, how far do you take the accelerated stall: impending or full?
check.a: Impending. You increase back pressure until an impending stall is reached, then recover at the first cue (ACS CA.VII.D.S5, S6).

body.p: A stall happens when the angle of attack goes past the wing's critical angle. Above that angle the air separates from the upper surface, burbles and eddies, lift drops and drag rises. Airspeed is not the cause. You can exceed the critical angle at any airspeed, attitude or power setting [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

Each airplane has one critical angle, roughly 16° to 20° depending on design, and it does not change with weight, load factor or density altitude. The stall speed, on the other hand, is not a fixed number [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
So the published 1 G stall speed only holds under four conditions [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]:

bullets: Unaccelerated, 1 G flight
Coordinated flight, ball centered
One weight, usually maximum gross
One CG position, usually the most forward

body.p: An accelerated stall breaks the first condition. In a turn or pull-up you ask the wing for more lift than the weight, and the only way it can make it at the same speed is with a higher angle of attack. That puts you closer to the critical angle, at a speed you think of as safe [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

callout.text: The wing reads angle of attack, not the airspeed indicator. Back pressure is the angle of attack control.

check.q: Name the four conditions under which a published 1 G stall speed is valid.
check.a: Unaccelerated 1 G flight, coordinated flight, one weight (usually max gross), and one CG (usually most forward) [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

chunks.title: Turns and pull-ups: why the stall speed climbs

body.p: There are two everyday ways to load the wing above 1 G. The first is a level turn: centrifugal force adds to weight, so the wing needs extra lift, which you get with back pressure and a higher angle of attack. If the angle gets too high at any point in the turn, the airplane stalls [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]] [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]].

The second is a sharp pull. In the PHAK example an airplane in a dive at 100 knots gets an abrupt pull on the elevator. Gravity and centrifugal force keep it moving along the old path for a moment, so the relative wind does not change direction as fast as the nose. The angle of attack jumps from low to very high, and the wing stalls at a speed far above the normal stall speed [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

How much faster? Stall speed grows with the square root of the load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. The figure below shows both curves against bank angle. They rise slowly at first and very fast past about 45° to 50° [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

head: Load on the wing
Stall speed of an airplane that stalls at 50 knots at 1 G
rows: 1 G, wings level
50 knots
About 1.4 G, level 45° bank
About 60 knots [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]
2 G, level 60° bank
About 70 knots [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]
4 G, hard pull

callout.text: The pilot who stalls at 70 knots in a turn was not slow. The load factor moved the stall speed up to meet the airspeed.

check.q: Your airplane stalls at 45 knots at 1 G. At what speed can it stall under 4 G?
check.a: 90 knots. The square root of 4 is 2, and 45 x 2 = 90 [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

chunks.title: Why the entry is at or below VA

body.p: VA is the highest speed at which the positive design limit load can be reached by a gust or by full deflection of one control surface without damage. At or below VA, a hard pull reaches the critical angle of attack first. The wing stalls, which unloads it, before the design load limit is reached. Above VA, the airplane can reach its design load limit before it reaches the critical angle, so you can keep pulling and overstress it [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

The Vg diagram shows this. The curved accelerated stall line is the most G the wing can make at each speed; above it the airplane simply stalls. Where that line meets the positive limit load factor is the maneuvering speed. Below that speed the wing cannot make a damaging positive load [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

bullets: VA goes down as weight goes down, so the max-gross number is too fast for a light airplane [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]] [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
VA does not protect you from rapid, large alternating inputs, or inputs in more than one axis; those can break the airplane even below VA [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]] [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
Intentional stalls practiced above VA can impose loads high enough to cause structural damage [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

callout.text: The ACS appendix for this Task says power must be set for an airspeed at or below VA (ACS Appendix 3, Task D). Know the published stall speed for 45° of bank, flaps up, before you fly it; it is typically in the AFM [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

check.q: Why is entering at or below VA what keeps the accelerated stall safe for the structure?
check.a: At or below VA the wing reaches the critical angle of attack and stalls, unloading itself, before the design limit load is reached [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

chunks.title: Weight, CG, power, configuration and yaw

body.p: The ACS asks you to tie the accelerated stall to angle of attack, airspeed, load factor, power, weight, CG, attitude and yaw (ACS CA.VII.D.K1). Here is what each one does:

head: Factor
Effect
rows: Weight
More weight needs a higher angle of attack for the same lift, so the stall speed goes up [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100i]].
Forward CG
The tail must push down harder, so the wing carries more load and stalls at a higher speed, with heavier back pressure needed [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]] [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100h]].
Aft CG

Less elevator force is needed to reach a stalling angle at a given load factor, so an inadvertent stall and high G come more easily. Recovery gets harder as the CG moves aft [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]] [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]].
Power
Propeller slipstream over the wing helps the recovery, but high power at a high angle of attack brings strong left yaw that needs right rudder [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
Flaps
Not used for this maneuver: lower design G limits [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Attitude
The stall can come at a lower pitch attitude than you expect, because the wing is loaded, not slow [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Yaw
If you are coordinated at the stall, both wings stall nearly together and the nose pitches away from you. If not, the bank angle may change until you reduce the angle of attack [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

callout.text: In a power-on accelerated stall to the left, torque and P-factor add to the yaw. Keep the ball centered all the way to the stall; that is what turns a 'bank change' into a clean nose drop.

check.q: You load the airplane near its aft CG limit. Why does that make an inadvertent accelerated stall more likely?
check.a: Less elevator force is needed to reach a stalling angle of attack at a given load factor, so it takes less pull to stall and to build high G [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]].

body.p: Design shapes how a wing stalls. Most trainers are built so the roots stall before the tips, using washout or stall strips, so the ailerons keep some effect [[24:120|AFH 5-15]] [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. Even so, using aileron before you reduce the angle of attack can deepen the stall on the low wing and roll you further [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

An accelerated stall in a coordinated, level turn behaves much like a wings-level stall, but the buffet can be sharper. Because it comes at a higher airspeed and sometimes a lower pitch attitude, it can catch an inexperienced pilot off guard [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Learn to recognize it by sight, sound and feel [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]:

bullets: Feel: the G pushes you down in the seat as you add back pressure [[24:124|AFH 5-19]], then buffet. Control pressures and reaction times change [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Sound: a stall horn or other warning device, and a change in the sound of the airflow [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Sight: the attitude is not a reliable cue, because the airplane can stall in any attitude [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

body.p: Limits of the warning: many stall warning devices alert about 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. Certification lets the warning come from natural buffet instead of a device, and many vintage, light-sport and experimental airplanes have no device at all [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. A warning system can fail, so you need the other cues too [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. With ice or other contamination the stall may come with little or none of the usual warning [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102]]. In uncoordinated flight the airspeed indicator and altimeter can be unreliable [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

callout.text: Part 23 requires controllable stall characteristics in straight, turning and accelerated turning flight, with a clear and distinctive stall warning that gives enough margin to prevent an inadvertent stall [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]].

check.q: Why is pitch attitude a poor cue for an accelerated stall?
check.a: The airplane can stall in any attitude, and accelerated stalls may come at lower pitch attitudes than expected [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: The single most important action in any stall recovery is to reduce the angle of attack. Pilots who put power or holding altitude first have lost control [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. The AFH gives a template adapted from one built by major airplane manufacturers; always use the POH procedure when it has one [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

head: Step
In a single-engine trainer
rows: 1. Autopilot or wing leveler: disconnect
Usually not installed, skip [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
2. Pitch nose-down until the stall warning stops (trim as needed)
Relax or release back pressure, push as needed [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
3. Roll wings level
Only after the angle of attack is reduced; cancel yaw with rudder [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
4. Power as needed
Promptly but smoothly, with rudder for the yaw [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
5. Speedbrakes or spoilers: retract
Usually not installed, skip [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
6. Return to the desired flightpath
Smooth, coordinated, avoiding a secondary stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]

body.p: In an accelerated stall the wing stalls because you are pulling. Often the recovery is mostly letting go of that pull. But do not overdo it: too much forward pressure can put a negative load on the wing and hinder the recovery [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]], and excessive forward elevator giving low or negative G is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

callout.text: Do not try to roll the wings level while the wing is still stalled. Reduce the angle of attack first, then roll. Adding power alone does not end a stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

body.p: On the checkride you acknowledge the cue out loud at the first indication, such as buffet or the horn (ACS CA.VII.D.S6), and recover using the POH procedure (ACS CA.VII.D.S7).

check.q: In the stall recovery template, which comes first: rolling wings level or reducing angle of attack?
check.a: Reducing angle of attack, until the stall warning stops. Then roll wings level [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

body.p: A secondary stall comes right after a recovery from the first one. The usual cause is pulling the nose up too soon and too hard, especially near the ground where the urge is strongest. It can also happen if you do not lower the pitch enough, or try to break the stall with power only [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. AC 61-67C puts it simply: hurrying the recovery before the airplane has regained enough flying speed [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].

Note that a secondary stall is itself an accelerated stall: you are pulling G at a speed that is not yet high enough to support it. The PHAK says a recovery that dives only to cruise or maneuvering speed, with a gradual pull as soon as the speed is safely above stall, can be done at no more than 2 or 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].
If one happens, do the same recovery again: nose-down pressure until the warning stops, wings level, coordinate, adjust power, then return to the flightpath [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

check.q: You recover from a stall and immediately haul the nose back to the horizon. The buffet returns. What happened, and what do you do?
check.a: A secondary stall from pulling up before flying speed returned [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]. Reduce the angle of attack again, level the wings, coordinate and adjust power [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

chunks.title: Cross-control stalls and the step into a spin

body.p: The deadliest accelerated stall is an uncoordinated one. A cross-control stall is when the critical angle is exceeded with aileron one way and rudder the other. It can come with very little warning; the nose may drop, the bank may change suddenly, and the airplane may keep rolling toward inverted, which is usually the beginning of a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

The classic setup is base to final. A tailwind on base pushes you past the centerline. You steepen the bank, pull, and press inside rudder to swing the nose around. The skid adds bank, the nose slices down, and the natural reaction is to pull harder. If the wing stalls with those inputs, the airplane may enter a spin quickly. The safest fix for an overshoot is a go-around, and you should be reluctant to use more than 30° of bank at that height [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

bullets: Skid (rudder into the turn): rotation goes the way the controls are applied [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

Slip (opposite aileron held against the rudder): the spin usually goes opposite the aileron [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]]. A slip that stalls shows little of the yawing that turns a skid into a spin, and may just roll toward wings level [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
Either way, a stall in a slipping or skidding turn can rotate in the direction of the rudder, regardless of which wingtip is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

body.p: A spin needs two things: a stall and yaw [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Yaw comes from rudder misuse, aileron adverse yaw, engine and propeller effects, or wind shear and wake [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Keeping the nose from yawing before you start the recovery is the key to avoiding a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. If one does start, the first turn costs about 1,000 ft and each later turn about half that [[24:128|AFH 5-23]], so a low-altitude spin is rarely survivable.

callout.text: In a turn near the ground, never use rudder to tighten the turn. If you are overshooting, go around [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

check.q: In a skidding turn to the left (left rudder, right aileron to hold the bank), the airplane stalls. Which way will it most likely roll into the spin?
check.a: To the left, the direction of the rudder, regardless of which wing is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]] [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

body.p: Accelerated stalls usually come from improperly flown turns, stall and spin recoveries, pullouts from steep dives, and base-to-final overshoots [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. The PHAK warns that this sudden loss of control in steep turns or abrupt back pressure near the ground has caused many accidents [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

head: Situation
How the stall comes
Prevention
rows: Base-to-final overshoot
Steep bank, back pressure and inside rudder [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Go around; keep bank modest; no skidding turns [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Turnback after engine failure
Not lowering the nose enough in the turn [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]
Know the altitude your airplane needs; get training first [[24:356|AFH 18-7]] [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Hurried round out
Pulling back too fast to avoid touching down early loads the wing [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Use power, or go around, instead of a sharp pull
Nose falls in a steep turn
Raising the nose without shallowing the bank tightens the turn toward a spiral [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]
Shallow the bank first, then raise the nose
Spiral dive recovery
Rolling and pulling at the same time at high speed [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Power idle, unload to about 1 G, roll level, then gently raise the nose [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]

body.p: Stall warnings during normal flight: when the horn or buffet comes on in a turn, a climb or the pattern, treat it as a stall that is about to happen. In the turnback case the AFH says to respond to any stall warning and reduce the load on the wing during the turn [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. Practicing slow flight teaches the same thing: any added angle of attack or load factor near the warning brings the warning, and you correct right away [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

callout.text: Turbulence can briefly set off the horn. The ACS treats a momentary activation in slow flight as acceptable if you recognize it and correct promptly (ACS Appendix 3, Task VII.A). The habit to build is the same: notice, unload, fix.

check.q: During a turnback after a simulated engine failure, the horn sounds halfway through the turn. What does the AFH tell you to do?
check.a: Respond to the stall warning and reduce the wing loading during the turn, which means lowering the nose and easing the back pressure or bank [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

body.p: Turbulence can stall the airplane at a much higher airspeed than in calm air. A vertical gust or wind shear suddenly changes the relative wind and raises the angle of attack. The gust may not last long enough to stall you, but you may stall while fighting to hold the flightpath, especially on a gusty approach [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. In rough air, slow to VA, and remember there may be gusts that exceed the load limits at any speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

A microburst can bring downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30 to 90 knots [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. The danger for this lesson is the reflex response: as the airplane sinks and loses speed, a pilot hauls back, which adds angle of attack at the worst moment. That last point is application, not a source rule.

High density altitude does not change the indicated stall speed, but your true airspeed is higher for the same indicated speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]], and performance drops as density altitude rises [[1:260|PHAK 11-4]]. Expect less power to help the recovery and more ground covered.

callout.text: Even a thin layer of frost, snow or ice raises the stall speed and can remove the normal stall warning. Do not fly with contamination on the wings [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100k]] [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102]].

check.q: At a high density altitude airport, does the indicated stall speed in a 45° bank go up, go down or stay the same?
check.a: It stays the same; altitude has little or no effect on indicated stall speed, though the true airspeed is higher [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]].

body.p: Before any stall practice, make sure the area at and below your altitude is clear and that you have enough height to recover [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Clearing turns exist to make sure the next maneuver will not take you into another aircraft's path [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. Scan in short, regularly spaced eye movements of no more than 10°, each held at least a second, and say the calls out loud: clear left, right, above and below [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

Distractions cause stalls. Looking for a checklist, working a windy pattern, reading a chart or reaching for something in the back seat all pull attention from airspeed and angle of attack [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]]. The ACS tells examiners to add realistic distractions to see how you divide attention (ACS Appendix 2, Use of Distractions).

In a 45° bank with your head inside, you can lose track of where you are and where the horizon is. Spatial illusions can make your senses disagree with the real attitude, and many upsets start while the pilot is busy with another task [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

callout.text: Pick your recovery heading and a ground reference before you roll in. After the recovery you will know at a glance where you are.

check.q: What does the PHAK say about how to scan for traffic?
check.a: Short, regularly spaced eye movements, each no more than 10°, with each area watched for at least 1 second [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

body.p: The AFH gives two entries. The common one starts straight and level at or below VA or VO, rolls into a coordinated level 45° turn, then increases angle of attack smoothly, firmly and progressively with back pressure. The other rolls in above VA and waits for the speed to drop to VA or below before pulling [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

bullets: Brief the numbers: VA for today's weight, the 45° flaps-up stall speed, VX and VY, and the altitude where you must be finished (ACS CA.VII.D.S2) [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Clear the area with clearing turns (ACS CA.VII.D.S1) [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
Set the configuration the examiner asks for, flaps up (ACS CA.VII.D.S3) [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Set power so the speed is at or below VA (ACS CA.VII.D.S4).
Roll into a coordinated 45° bank and hold it with the ball centered (ACS CA.VII.D.S5).
Add back pressure smoothly and firmly. Feel the G push you into the seat; airspeed may drop as drag rises [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
At the first buffet or horn, say 'stall' and recover: reduce angle of attack, roll wings level, add power, coordinate (ACS CA.VII.D.S6, S7) [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Set the POH configuration and accelerate to VX or VY (ACS CA.VII.D.S8), then return to the assigned altitude, heading and airspeed (ACS CA.VII.D.S9).

callout.text: Recover from the climb gently. A brisk pull back to the horizon after the stall is exactly the move that makes a secondary stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

check.q: What three things does S9 ask you to return to after the recovery?
check.a: The altitude, heading and airspeed specified by the evaluator (ACS CA.VII.D.S9).

body.p: These come from the AFH list of common stall errors [[24:126|AFH 5-21]], with the fix for each:

head: Error
Fix
rows: Not clearing the area well
Clearing turns and a spoken scan every time
Bank angle not held constant in the turn
Pick a bank picture on the horizon; check the attitude indicator
Poor coordination through the stall and recovery
Ball centered before the pull; rudder for yaw as power comes in
Trying to level the wings before reducing angle of attack
Unload first, then roll [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Recovering with power before reducing angle of attack
Nose-down pressure first; power is step four [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Not holding nose-down input until the warning stops
Keep the pressure until the horn and buffet are gone
Secondary stall in the recovery
Gradual pull, only once speed is safely above stall [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]
Too much forward pressure, low or negative G
Unload to about 1 G, not to zero
Excessive airspeed in the recovery
Bring the nose up gently once flying, and watch for VA and the redline
Failing to return to the flightpath
Know the assigned altitude, heading and airspeed before you start

callout.text: The AFH also lists an inadvertent accelerated stall from pulling too fast during the entry to a power-off or power-on stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Keep that in mind on the other stall Tasks.

check.q: Your CFI says your accelerated stall recovery 'went negative'. What error is that, and what is the fix?
check.a: Excessive forward elevator giving low or negative G [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Reduce the angle of attack only enough to stop the stall warning, about back to 1 G [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].

f1.caption: Figure 5-38. Forces exerted when pulling out of a dive. (PHAK 5-26)
f1.alt: An airplane comes down a steep dotted path from upper right and levels off near the ground at lower left. At each point blue arrows show lift (L) and weight (W) and a yellow arrow shows centrifugal force (CF). Near the bottom of the pull-out, centrifugal force points straight down, adding to weight, and the lift arrow is long.

f2.caption: Figure 5-39. Increase in stall speed and load factor. (PHAK 5-26)
f2.alt: A graph against bank angle from 0 to 90 degrees. A red curve shows the percent increase in stall speed and a black curve shows load factor in G. Both stay low through about 40 degrees, then rise more and more steeply; the red curve passes 100 percent at about 75 degrees and the black curve reaches 13 G near 85 degrees.

f3.caption: Figure 5-55. Typical Vg diagram. (PHAK 5-38)
f3.alt: A chart of load factor from minus 3 to plus 7 against indicated airspeed in mph. A red curve labeled accelerated stall rises from the normal stall speed point near 64 mph at 1 G to the maneuvering speed point near 137 mph at about 4.4 G. A green normal operating range lies below it, a yellow caution range lies to the right of the maximum structural cruise speed line, and orange and red zones mark structural damage and failure above the limit load and beyond the never-exceed speed.

f4.caption: Figure 5-13. Secondary stall. (AFH 5-19)
f4.alt: A high-wing airplane flies a yellow path from left to right. At the initial stall the nose rises and the path curves down. An incomplete or improper recovery pulls the nose back up too soon, and the path curves down again into a secondary stall, ending lower and nose-down near the hills.

f5.alt: Three rear views of a banked airplane. Normal turn: centrifugal force equals horizontal lift. Slipping turn: centrifugal force is less than horizontal lift. Skidding turn: centrifugal force is greater than horizontal lift, and the load arrow leans toward the outside of the turn.

f6.alt: A yellow ribbon winds in a corkscrew around a tall vertical pole. At the bottom, a high-wing airplane descends nose-down along the ribbon, rotating around the pole.

f7.alt: Three panels of the same airfoil in a flowing blue airstream. A: 10 degrees angle of attack with smooth flow over the top. B: 16 degrees, with flow starting to break up into small swirls behind the trailing edge. C: 17 degrees, with large swirling eddies over the whole upper surface.

scenario.title: The checkride accelerated stall on a bumpy, warm afternoon
scenario.setup: You are on your commercial checkride in a four-seat, fixed-pitch trainer with the examiner and half fuel, well below maximum weight. The POH lists VA as 105 KIAS at maximum weight and 95 KIAS at a weight close to yours. The practice area's terrain is about 1,500 ft MSL, it is a hot afternoon with light to moderate thermal bumps, and a flight school uses the same area. The examiner says: 'Show me a power-off accelerated stall to the left, clean, when you are ready.' Partway through the setup the examiner asks you to find the nearest airport on the chart.

questions.q: What is the lowest altitude at which you may finish the maneuver, and how do you choose your entry altitude?
questions.a: No lower than 3,000 ft AGL, so 4,500 ft MSL here (ACS CA.VII.D.S2), with room above that for the recovery and climb. Some altitude loss in a stall recovery is expected [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

questions.q: Which VA do you respect, and why not the 105-knot figure?
questions.a: The lighter-weight figure, about 95 KIAS. VA goes down as weight goes down [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]], and the ACS asks for power set so airspeed does not exceed VA (ACS CA.VII.D.S4).

questions.q: The bumps set off the stall horn for a moment while you are still setting up. What does that tell you, and what do you do?
questions.a: A vertical gust can raise the angle of attack suddenly and stall the airplane at a higher airspeed than in calm air [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. Unload, check speed and coordination, and stay at or below VA in the turbulence [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

questions.q: The examiner's chart question comes as you roll into the turn. How do you handle it?
questions.a: Fly first: hold the bank and coordination, or roll out and answer before restarting. Distractions such as reading a chart are a classic cause of stalls [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]], and the ACS lets the examiner add them on purpose (ACS Appendix 2).

questions.q: Just as the buffet starts, the left wing drops and the bank steepens. What happened and how do you recover?
questions.a: The airplane was probably not coordinated at the stall, so the bank changed [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Reduce the angle of attack first, then level the wings with aileron and rudder, then add power [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Do not use aileron before unloading; it can deepen the stall on the low wing [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

questions.q: After the recovery the airspeed is building and you are 300 ft below entry. How do you get back without another stall?
questions.a: Pull gradually, only once the speed is safely above stall; a hurried pull-up causes a secondary stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]] [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. Then accelerate to VX or VY and return to the assigned altitude, heading and airspeed (ACS CA.VII.D.S8, S9).

skills.practice: Fly two clearing turns and call 'clear left, right, above and below' before every stall [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

skills.do: Pick an entry altitude that lets you finish the whole Task no lower than 3,000 ft AGL.
skills.practice: Before each flight, write the terrain height plus 3,000 ft on your kneeboard as your floor, and enter well above it.

skills.do: Set up the configuration the examiner asks for.
skills.practice: Practice both clean power-off and clean power-on entries; never with flaps for this maneuver [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

skills.do: Set power so the airspeed does not go above VA or any other POH/AFM limit.
skills.practice: Look up VA for your actual weight and say it out loud before you roll in [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

skills.do: Hold a coordinated 45° bank and increase back pressure smoothly and firmly until an impending stall.
skills.practice: Practice holding a steady 45° bank with the ball centered, then add back pressure in one smooth, steady motion [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

skills.do: Say what you notice at the first sign of a stall, such as buffet or the stall horn.
skills.practice: Call 'buffet' or 'horn' the moment you sense it, so recognition and recovery become one motion [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

skills.do: Recover using the POH procedure: reduce angle of attack, wings level, power, coordinated.
skills.practice: Chair-fly the template until the order is automatic: unload, roll, power, return [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

skills.do: Configure the airplane as the manufacturer recommends and accelerate to VX or VY.
skills.practice: Brief VX and VY before each stall and fly to the target speed after every recovery.

skills.do: Return to the altitude, heading and airspeed the examiner gave you.
skills.practice: Have your CFI give a heading and altitude before each stall and grade your return to them.

quiz.q: What G-load defines an accelerated maneuver stall?
options: Any stall above +1 G
Only stalls above 2 G
Any stall with the flaps up
Only stalls with power on
quiz.why: Stalls encountered any time the G-load exceeds +1 G are called accelerated maneuver stalls [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

quiz.q: Which of these does NOT change the critical angle of attack of a given wing?
options: Load factor
Ice on the leading edge
Snow on the upper surface
Frost on the wing
quiz.why: A given aircraft always stalls at the same critical angle regardless of airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. Ice, snow or frost cause separation at an angle lower than the critical angle [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say about flaps for accelerated stall practice?
options: Never extended, because design G limits are lower with flaps
Half flaps, to lower the stall speed
Full flaps, to simulate a landing
Any setting the instructor prefers
quiz.why: A pilot should never practice accelerated stalls with the flaps extended due to the lower design G-load limits in that configuration [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

quiz.q: On the Vg diagram, what does the curved line labeled 'accelerated stall' show?
options: The most load factor the wing can produce at each airspeed
The never-exceed speed
The structural limit load factor
The speed for best glide
quiz.why: It is the line of maximum lift capability; any load factor above it is unavailable because the airplane stalls [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]] [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]].

quiz.q: With the CG moved aft, what happens to the elevator force needed to stall at a given load factor?
options: It goes down
It goes up
It does not change
It reverses direction
quiz.why: As the CG moves aft, less elevator deflection and force are needed to stall at a given load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]].

quiz.q: In a coordinated, level-turn accelerated stall, how does the airplane usually behave?
options: The nose pitches away from you, much like a wings-level stall, with a possibly sharper buffet
It always snaps into a spin
It rolls inverted
It climbs because of the extra lift
quiz.why: If coordinated at the stall, both wings stall nearly together and the nose pitches away from the pilot; the buffet can be sharper [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

quiz.q: About how far ahead of the stall do many stall warning devices sound?
options: 4 to 8 knots
1 to 2 knots
15 to 20 knots
Exactly at the stall
quiz.why: Many aircraft have stall warning devices that alert the pilot 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

quiz.q: What is the primary cause of an inadvertent spin, according to AC 61-67C?
options: Exceeding the critical angle of attack with too much or too little rudder
Too much airspeed in a dive
Flying near VA
Using carburetor heat in a stall
quiz.why: The primary cause is exceeding the critical AOA while applying excessive or insufficient rudder and, to a lesser extent, aileron [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

quiz.q: In the AFH secondary stall discussion, what besides pulling up too soon can cause one?
options: Trying to break the stall with power only
Using right rudder
Keeping the wings level
Holding forward pressure too long
quiz.why: A secondary stall can happen when the pilot does not reduce AOA enough by lowering the pitch, or tries to break the stall with power only [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

quiz.q: Altitude and temperature change which of these?
options: True airspeed for a given indicated airspeed
Indicated stall speed
Critical angle of attack
Load factor in a 45° bank
quiz.why: Thin or warm air gives a higher true airspeed for a given indicated airspeed, but it has little or no effect on indicated stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]]. The critical angle does not change with density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH VA at max weight is 110 KIAS. Today you are 400 lb lighter and the POH gives 99 KIAS for that weight. You roll into the accelerated stall at 106 KIAS. What is the problem?
options: You are above VA for today's weight, so the airplane can reach its limit load before it stalls
Nothing, 106 is below the 110-knot VA
You are too slow to reach a stall
The stall horn will not work above 100 knots
final_quiz.why: VA is lower at lower weight [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. Above VA the airplane can reach its design load limit at less than the critical AOA and be overstressed [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. The ACS limit is VA (ACS CA.VII.D.S4).

final_quiz.q: Terrain under the practice area is 2,200 ft MSL. What is the lowest altitude at which the checkride accelerated stall may be completed?
options: 5,200 ft MSL
3,700 ft MSL
3,000 ft MSL
4,200 ft MSL
final_quiz.why: No lower than 3,000 ft AGL (ACS CA.VII.D.S2): 2,200 + 3,000 = 5,200 ft MSL. The 1,500 ft AGL figure in the AFH is for general stall practice [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], not this Task.

final_quiz.q: Halfway through a 45° accelerated stall entry the buffet starts and the right wing drops sharply. You were holding a little left rudder. What is the best first action?
options: Release back pressure and push as needed to reduce the angle of attack
Full left aileron to pick up the wing
Full power, then level the wings
More back pressure to stop the nose dropping
final_quiz.why: Reduce the AOA first; leveling the wings before the AOA is reduced can make the stall worse on the low wing [[24:120|AFH 5-15]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Uncoordinated flight at the stall can change the bank angle [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: An older airplane stalls at 60 knots. The pilot stalls it with a hard pull at 102 knots. About what load factor did the wing reach?
options: About 2.9 G
About 1.7 G
About 4.4 G
About 6 G
final_quiz.why: Load factor equals the square of the speed ratio: 102 / 60 = 1.7, and 1.7 x 1.7 = 2.89 G [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

final_quiz.q: On base you are carrying a tailwind and realize you will overshoot the centerline. Which action fits the AFH guidance?
options: Go around
Add inside rudder to swing the nose around
Steepen to 50° and pull harder
Hold opposite aileron and inside rudder to keep the bank shallow
final_quiz.why: The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around; avoid more than 30° of bank at that height and never make a skidding turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: You recover from a stall and the airspeed is climbing through VA in a steep nose-down attitude. Which recovery is most likely to over-stress the airplane?
options: Pulling hard back to level while rolling level at the same time
Reducing power and leveling the wings, then raising the nose gently
Unloading to about 1 G before rolling level
Raising the nose only after the speed comes down
final_quiz.why: Rolling and pulling together is a listed spiral dive recovery error, and the design limit is exceeded more easily in a rolling pullout [[24:131|AFH 5-26]] [[24:132|AFH 5-27]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement about the stall warning in a contaminated (iced) airplane is correct?
options: The stall may come with little or none of the usual warning
The warning comes earlier, so you get more margin
Ice only changes the stall speed, not the warning
The horn works normally because it senses angle of attack
final_quiz.why: In some icing conditions an aerodynamic stall may occur with little or none of the usual cues, such as buffet or the stall horn [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102]].

final_quiz.q: In a slipping turn to the left (left aileron held, right rudder), the airplane stalls and starts to spin. Which way will it usually rotate?
options: To the right, opposite the aileron
To the left, toward the aileron
It cannot spin from a slip
Straight down without rotation
final_quiz.why: In a slipping turn, with opposite aileron held against the rudder, the spin usually goes opposite the aileron being applied [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]], which is the direction of the rudder [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the PHAK say the load factor in a proper spin recovery is usually higher than in a stall recovery?
options: The nose is much lower, so the speed and the pull-out load are higher
Spins happen above VA
The spin itself is flown at high G
Flaps are always down in a spin
final_quiz.why: Spin recoveries usually happen with the nose much lower than in stall recoveries, so higher airspeeds and higher load factors follow, about 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. In the spin itself the load is only slightly above 1 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

final_quiz.q: You are flying in moderate turbulence near your practice area. What speed guidance does AC 61-67C give for cruise?
options: Well above the stall speed and below maneuvering speed
At VNE to get through quickly
At the 1 G stall speed plus 5 knots
At best glide speed
final_quiz.why: In cruise in moderate or severe turbulence, use an airspeed well above the indicated stall speed and below maneuvering speed, remembering VA is lower at lower weight [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

final_quiz.q: You are rounding out too late for a landing and haul the yoke back to avoid touching down on the nose wheel. What risk does the AFH name?
options: An accelerated stall from the sudden wing load
A tail strike only
A ground loop
Engine overspeed
final_quiz.why: Starting the round out too late or pulling back too rapidly can impose a significant load on the wings and cause an accelerated stall [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

final_quiz.q: An airplane certificated under today's Part 23 standards must show what about stalls in accelerated turning flight?
options: Controllable stall characteristics with a clear, distinctive stall warning
That it cannot stall in a turn
Recovery from a six-turn spin
A stall horn that sounds 10 knots early
final_quiz.why: 14 CFR 23.2150(a) requires controllable stall characteristics in straight, turning and accelerated turning flight, with a clear and distinctive stall warning giving enough margin [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]].

final_quiz.q: The examiner asks why an accelerated stall can surprise a pilot even when the stall horn works. Best answer?
options: It comes at a higher airspeed and maybe a lower pitch attitude than the pilot expects
The horn is disabled above 1 G
It only happens with flaps down
It always happens without buffet
final_quiz.why: Accelerated stalls occur at higher-than-normal airspeeds or at lower-than-anticipated pitch attitudes, so they can surprise an inexperienced pilot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

takeaways: A wing stalls at its critical angle of attack, at any speed; load factor just moves the stall speed up.
Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor: 4 G doubles it.
Enter at or below VA for today's weight, flaps up, about 45° of bank, finished no lower than 3,000 ft AGL.
On the checkride: coordinated 45° bank, smooth firm back pressure, recover at the first cue.
Recovery: unload first, then wings level, then power, then a gentle climb to VX or VY.
A hurried pull-up after recovery is a secondary stall; a stall with yaw is the start of a spin.
Real accelerated stalls happen in overshooting turns, turnbacks, hurried round outs and dive pullouts; go around instead of pulling.
cfi_notes: The ACS floor for this Task is 3,000 ft AGL (ACS CA.VII.D.S2), while the AFH's general stall guidance and AC 61-67C 103 use 1,500 ft AGL for single-engine stall practice [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. Teach the ACS number for accelerated stalls; the AFH's multiengine chapter uses 3,000 ft AGL for the same maneuver [[24:269|AFH 13-20]].

The ACS asks for an impending stall only (ACS CA.VII.D.S5), while the AFH describes the maneuver to a full stall and says to recover at the first indication if impending stall training [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Make sure the student's habit matches the test.

AC 61-67C 105 says the next step after reducing AOA is to smoothly apply maximum allowable power [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]. The newer AFH template puts wings level before power and says power 'as needed' [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Teach the AFH order and the POH.

AC 61-67C 108 cites 14 CFR 23.221(a) for the one-turn spin margin [[13:12|AC 61-67C 108]]. That section is gone; current Part 23 is performance based and stalls and spins are in 14 CFR 23.2150 [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]]. Teach the idea, cite the current rule.

PHAK 5-36 says 112 knots gives 4 G in an airplane that stalls at 60 knots [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. The square-root rule gives (112 / 60) squared = 3.5 G; 4 G needs 120 knots. Its Vg diagram numbers also run a bit high (92, 112 and 137 mph versus 90.5, 111 and 134 by the formula) [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. Teach the formula.

The AFH second entry method says to pull 'at an airspeed 5 to 10 percent faster than the unaccelerated stall speed' after slowing to VA [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Read literally, that speed is far below VA and would not be a 45° accelerated stall. Treat the wording as unclear and fly the common method from at or below VA.

AFH 5-9 says a 2 G turn raises stall speed 41 percent [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] and AC 61-67C 100b says 40 percent [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100b]]. Both are the square root of 2, rounded; do not let students get stuck on it.

PHAK 5-37 says no combination of maneuver and gust can cause damage below maneuvering speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]], but AC 61-67C 100f and PHAK 5-35 say large alternating or multi-axis inputs can cause failure even below VA [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]] [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Teach the more cautious wording.

Students tend to fly the pull too slowly and run out of airspeed in a mushing turn, or too abruptly and get a sharp break. Demonstrate the feel of the G in the seat first, at a safe altitude, then let the student match it [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
gaps: The 45° bank flaps-up stall speed, VA at the actual weight, and any manufacturer entry speed for accelerated stalls come from the POH/AFM [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. None is given here.

The ACS gives no plus or minus tolerance on the 45° bank and no altitude loss limit for this Task; the examiner judges both. The ACS appendix gives 'no predetermined altitude loss' guidance only for power-off and power-on stalls.
No single-engine source here gives a rate for the slowdown during the pull; the only figure, about 3 to 5 knots per second, is in the AFH multiengine chapter [[24:269|AFH 13-20]]. Use CFI technique.
The sources say flap-extended design G limits are lower [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] but give no numbers. Check the POH/AFM.
No source here gives a small-airplane recovery technique for an accelerated stall inside a microburst or wind shear encounter; the microburst material is general [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
Whether a brief stall warning during a normal landing flare is expected depends on the airplane; the sources do not address it. Ask your CFI and check the POH.

activities.title: Read the angle of attack panels
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Smooth airflow following the upper surface
Angle between the chord line and the relative wind
Flow beginning to break away behind the trailing edge
Burbling, separated flow: lift drops, drag rises
An angle past the critical angle of attack

activities.title: Does it raise the indicated stall speed?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Steepening a level turn from 30° to 45°
An abrupt pull-up from a dive
Frost on the upper wing surface
A hot day at a high-elevation airport
Flying the same maneuver at a lighter weight

activities.title: Work the accelerated stall numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your airplane stalls at 50 KIAS at 1 G, clean. You pull as hard as you can at 90 KIAS. What is the most load factor the wing can make before it stalls? (Use the speed ratio squared.)
items.why: 90 / 50 = 1.8. 1.8 x 1.8 = 3.24 G. Load factor goes with the square of the speed increase [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. That is under the 3.8 G normal-category limit [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]], so the wing stalls first.

items.q: Same airplane, 1 G stall 50 KIAS, normal category limit 3.8 G. At about what speed could a hard pull just reach the limit load? (Stall speed x square root of 3.8.)
items.why: Square root of 3.8 = 1.949. 50 x 1.949 = 97.5 KIAS. That is the point on a Vg diagram where the accelerated stall line meets the limit load: the maneuvering speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]].

items.q: After a stall recovery you pull out at 2.5 G. Your 1 G stall speed is 48 KIAS. Below what speed will that pull cause a secondary stall?
items.why: Square root of 2.5 = 1.581. 48 x 1.581 = 75.9, about 76 KIAS [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. PHAK 5-36 says a gradual pull of 2 to 2.5 G once safely above stall is enough [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

items.q: Terrain in the practice area is 1,800 ft MSL. You expect the recovery to cost up to 300 ft. What is the lowest altitude you should start the maneuver?
items.why: Floor: 1,800 + 3,000 = 4,800 ft MSL (ACS CA.VII.D.S2). Add the 300 ft you expect to lose: 4,800 + 300 = 5,100 ft MSL. Some altitude loss in recovery is expected [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

items.q: An accelerated stall turns into an accidental spin that runs three full turns before it stops. About how much altitude does it take?
items.why: First turn about 1,000 ft, each later turn about half that: 1,000 + 500 + 500 = 2,000 ft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

activities.title: True or false: recognition and recovery
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Adding power typically reduces altitude loss in a stall recovery, but it does not by itself end the stall.
cards.why: True. Power reduces altitude loss but does not eliminate a stall; reducing AOA is imperative [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

cards.s: If a wing drops at the stall, pick it up with opposite aileron before doing anything else.
cards.why: False. Aileron used before reducing AOA can make the low wing stall more completely and roll further [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

cards.s: Most training airplanes are designed so the wingtips stall before the roots.
cards.why: False. Most are designed so the wings stall from the roots outward, keeping some aileron effect [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

cards.s: Certification lets the stall warning come from natural buffet instead of a warning device.
cards.why: True. Manufacturers may provide the required warning through pre-stall buffeting or a device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

cards.s: Snapping the elevator forward in a recovery can produce negative load factors.
cards.why: True. Snapping the elevator control forward can produce negative load factors [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

cards.s: In a spin, the indicated airspeed keeps building.
cards.why: False. In a spin the airspeed is low and roughly constant; if it is increasing, the airplane is no longer spinning [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

activities.title: Put the accelerated stall in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Brief VA for the weight, the 45° stall speed, VX or VY and the 3,000 ft AGL floor
Clear the area with clearing turns
Set the configuration (flaps up) and power for a speed at or below VA
Increase back pressure smoothly and firmly
Call the first stall cue and reduce the angle of attack
Roll wings level, add power, stay coordinated
Accelerate to VX or VY and return to the assigned altitude, heading and airspeed

activities.title: Name that stall or upset
activities.intro: Tap a description, then the name that fits it.

pairs.l: Pulling the nose up before flying speed returns after a recovery
Inside rudder, opposite aileron and back pressure in an overshooting turn
A sharp pull from a 100-knot dive stalls the wing far above normal stall speed
Stalled and yawed, following a downward corkscrew path
Nose-low, wing-low descending turn, not stalled, speed and G building

activities.title: Accelerated stall practice, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are flying a four-seat trainer solo to practice for your commercial checkride. You are light: one pilot and half fuel. The practice area is over terrain about 1,200 ft MSL, with scattered cumulus and some bumps under them.

steps.s: You level off at 3,800 ft MSL and get ready for your first accelerated stall.
options: Climb so you have room above 4,200 ft MSL for the recovery before starting
Start now; the stall will only cost 100 ft
Start now and recover at the first cue to save altitude
Descend to 3,000 ft MSL to stay clear of the clouds
steps.why: The Task must be finished no lower than 3,000 ft AGL: 1,200 + 3,000 = 4,200 ft MSL (ACS CA.VII.D.S2). Some altitude loss in recovery is expected [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

steps.s: Your POH gives VA 104 KIAS at max weight and 94 KIAS near your weight. Cruise is 110 KIAS.
options: Slow to 94 KIAS or below before rolling in
Use 104 KIAS; it is in the POH
Roll in at cruise and pull right away
Slow to the 1 G stall speed, then roll in
steps.why: VA is lower at lower weight [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]; above VA the airplane can reach its design limit before it stalls [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. The AFH's other method waits for the speed to drop to VA before pulling [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

steps.s: In the 45° bank you add back pressure. The ball drifts to the inside of the turn as the horn sounds.
options: Reduce angle of attack, then level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder
Hold the back pressure and fix the ball with rudder first
Add full power and keep turning
Roll level with aileron alone, keeping the back pressure
steps.why: Recover at the first cue by reducing AOA first [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Uncoordinated flight at the stall can change the bank [[24:125|AFH 5-20]], and a stall in a slip or skid can lead to a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

steps.s: The recovery worked, the nose is 10° down and speed is building through 85 KIAS. You want your altitude back.
options: Raise the nose gradually to a VY climb
Pull firmly back to the horizon right now
Push further to gain more speed
Roll into a steep turn to slow down
steps.why: A hurried pull-up before enough speed returns causes a secondary stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]. A gradual pull once safely above stall needs no more than 2 to 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

steps.s: On the second try a thermal bump hits as you near the stall, and the buffet comes earlier and harder than before.
options: Recover, and move to smoother air or higher before trying again
Pull harder to get through the bump
Keep practicing; turbulence makes good training
Lower the flaps to soften the stall
steps.why: A vertical gust can raise the AOA and stall the airplane at a higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]]. Flaps are never used for accelerated stalls [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
